studies.Population: men admitted to hospital (cases with prostate cancer; controls with acute nonneoplastic diseases)
studies.comparison_type: more than eight alcoholic beverages per day vs teetotallers

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: The relationship between prostate cancer and total alcohol consumption was therefore investigated in a case-control study conducted in Northern Italy between 1985 and 1992 on 281 cases and 599 controls admitted to hospital for acute nonneoplastic diseases apparently unrelated to alcohol and tobacco consumption. No noteworthy relationship was found for major measures of alcohol intake: compared with teetotallers, the multivariate relative risks (RRs) of prostate cancer, after adjustment for age, study center, education, marital status, body mass index, and smoking status, were 1.3, 0.9, 1.2, and 1.1, respectively, for men drinking fewer than three, three to less than five, five to less than eight, or more than eight alcoholic beverages per day.
extraction_supporting_text.cases: The relationship between prostate cancer and total alcohol consumption was therefore investigated in a case-control study conducted in Northern Italy between 1985 and 1992 on 281 cases and 599 controls admitted to hospital for acute nonneoplastic diseases apparently unrelated to alcohol and tobacco consumption.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: None of the estimates was significant, nor was the trend in risk significant. Multivariate risks were also close to unity in the separate analysis of intake of wine (RR = 1.2 and 0.9 for < 5 and or = 5 drinks/day, respectively, compared with wine abstainers), beer (RR = 1.1 for beer drinkers compared with beer abstainers), and spirit (RR = 0.8 for spirit intake compared with beer abstainers).

studies.Population: Men aged 55 years or older in the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial with end-of-study biopsy data
studies.Ethnicity Basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available
studies.Reference: Alcohol consumption, finasteride, and prostate cancer risk: results from the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial.
studies.Authors: Gong Z, Kristal AR, Schenk JM, Tangen CM, Goodman PJ, Thompson IM
studies.Design: Prospective cohort analysis nested within a randomized placebo-controlled trial
studies.Timing: Alcohol intake was assessed at baseline and prostate cancer was detected during the 7-year trial period
studies.comparison_type: Heavy alcohol consumption (≥50 g/day) versus no alcohol consumption for high-grade prostate cancer, combined treatment arms
studies.direction_imputation_reason: Comparison direction was not explicit; the protocol assumes high versus low exposure.
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants reported the frequency of consuming each type of beverage (beer, wine, and liquor) over the past year in 7 categories (“never”, “1 day/month”, “2-3 days/month”, “1-2 days/week”, “3-4 days/week”, “5-6 days/week” or “every day”).

sample_size.excerpt: Among the total 10,920 men in this analysis, 2,129 (19.5%) men were diagnosed with prostate cancer (1,425 (66.9%) Gleason score 2-6; 564 (26.5%) Gleason score 7 or higher; and 140 (6.5%) Gleason score unknown). Among the 2,129 cases, 1,515 (71.2%) were stage T1, 505 (23.7%) were stage T2, 37 (1.7%) were stage T3 and 72 (3.4%) were unknown stage.
sample_size.location: Materials and Methods, Study Design and Study Population, final paragraph

cases.excerpt: Data for this study came from the 2129 participants in the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT) who had cancer detected during the 7-year trial and 8791 men who were determined by biopsy to be free of cancer at the trial end.

effect_size.excerpt: In combined arms, heavy alcohol consumption (> or =50 g of alcohol daily) and regular heavy drinking (> or =4 drinks daily on > or =5 days per week) were associated with increased risks of high-grade prostate cancer (RR, 2.01 [95% CI, 1.33-3.05] and 2.17 [95% CI, 1.42-3.30], respectively); less heavy drinking was not associated with risk.

confidence_interval.excerpt: In combined arms, heavy alcohol consumption (> or =50 g of alcohol daily) and regular heavy drinking (> or =4 drinks daily on > or =5 days per week) were associated with increased risks of high-grade prostate cancer (RR, 2.01 [95% CI, 1.33-3.05] and 2.17 [95% CI, 1.42-3.30], respectively); less heavy drinking was not associated with risk.

comparison.excerpt: In a post-hoc analysis, the relative risk for high-grade cancer associated with heavy drinking in the combined study arms was 2.01

design.excerpt: All data for this study were collected as part of the PCPT, a randomized, placebo-controlled trial
design.location: Materials and Methods, Study Design and Study Population, first paragraph

timing.excerpt: Details regarding age, race, education, diabetes status, family history of prostate cancer in first-degree relatives, physical activity, history of smoking, and usual alcohol consumption were collected at baseline using self-administered questionnaires.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test indicates significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.0052) for the meta-analysis of Alcohol and Prostate cancer\aggressive. This finding suggests the presence of small-study effects, which may arise from publication bias or other sources of heterogeneity related to study size. The pooled estimate should therefore be interpreted with appropriate caution.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 26 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.2 (95% CI: 1.1–1.31), suggesting that alcohol is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer\aggressive. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was very high between-study heterogeneity (I² = 86.87%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
